Conditions and time limits:
- The complaint must be in writing and made by the payee or the holder in due course within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].

rows.question: Is there a legal presumption in favour of the holder of a cheque?
queries: Is there a legal presumption in favour of the holder of a cheque?

Furthermore, as noted in the Supreme Court judgment in Basalingappa versus Mudibasappa, the complainant being the holder of the cheque and the signature on the cheque not being denied by the accused, a presumption shall be drawn that the cheque was issued for the discharge of any debt or other liability, which is a rebuttable presumption [12].

rows.question: What makes an agreement a valid contract?
queries: What makes an agreement a valid contract?

rows.answer:
An agreement becomes a contract if it is made by the free consent of parties who are competent to contract, for a lawful consideration, with a lawful object, and is not expressly declared by law to be void, as stated in Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

Related provisions:
- Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which covers "Who are competent to contract" [2].
- Section 13 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which defines "Consent" [4].
- Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which covers "What considerations and objects are lawful, and what not" [5].

Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake subject to the provisions of sections 20, 21, and 22 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12]. Consent is considered so caused when it would not have been given but for the existence of such coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake [1].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?

rows.answer:
A contract can be avoided when consent to the agreement is caused by coercion or misrepresentation, making it a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused, as provided in Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

As discussed by the Supreme Court in the judgment "M/S. N.N. GLOBAL MERCANTILE PVT. LTD. versus M/S. INDO UNIQUE FLAME LTD. & OTHERS", such an agreement remains enforceable and is not void until it is proved and upheld as voidable [13]. 

Conditions and time limits:
- The consent must have been caused by coercion or misrepresentation, meaning it would not have been given but for that coercion or misrepresentation, under Section 14 and Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][3].

rows.answer: Fraud that makes a contract voidable includes any of the following acts committed by a party to a contract, or with his connivance, or by his agent, with intent to deceive another party thereto or his agent, or to induce him to enter into the contract: the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true; the active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of the fact; a promise made without any intention of performing it; any other act fitted to deceive; and any such act or omission as the law specially declares to be fraudulent, under Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. Mere silence as to facts likely to affect the willingness of a person to enter into a contract is not fraud, unless the circumstances of the case are such that, regard being had to them, it is the duty of the person keeping silence to speak, or unless his silence is, in itself, equivalent to speech, according to Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?

Indian Contract Act section 12 unsound mind
topSources: The Indian Council of World Affairs Act, 2001 s1

rows.answer:
Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which they are subject, who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which they are subject, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12]. A person is considered to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract if, at the time of making it, they are capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon their interests, according to Section 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [2][12].

Related provisions:

As stated in Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the party complaining of the breach is entitled to receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the penalty stipulated for, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused [1]. This is also supported by the Supreme Court judgment in "B.S.N.L versus RELIANCE COMMUNICATION LTD." and the Supreme Court judgment in "M/S. Exceptions to this rule and related provisions where restraints are permitted or agreements are not void include:

rows.question: How far is a surety liable for the debt of the principal debtor?
queries: How far is a surety liable for the debt of the principal debtor?

Indian Contract Act section 128 surety liability

rows.answer:
The liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. For instance, where a bill of exchange is guaranteed and subsequently dishonoured, the surety is liable not only for the amount of the bill, but also for any interest and charges that may have become due on it under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. Furthermore, as discussed in the Supreme Court judgment "Bank of Bihar Ltd. versus Damodar Prasad & Anr.", the surety's liability is immediate upon demand being fulfilled, and it is not deferred until the creditor exhausts remedies against the principal debtor [13].

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?

rows.answer:
Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine, according to Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [5]. Similarly, Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 provides that whoever commits murder shall be punished with death, or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine [1]. Furthermore, when a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [5]. Additionally, whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life, according to Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [9]. Under Section 303 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder shall be punished with death [8].

rows.question: What is dowry death and its punishment?

rows.answer:
Dowry death occurs when the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or happens otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage, and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry [1][3][12]. In such cases, the husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused her death, as provided under Section 304B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 80 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1][3]. For these provisions, "dowry" has the same meaning as in section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 [1][3].

Whoever commits dowry death shall be punished with imprisonment for a term of not less than seven years, which may extend to imprisonment for life, under Section 304B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 80 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1][3].

A sale of immovable property is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised, according to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. To constitute a sale, there must be a transfer of ownership from one person to another where all rights and interests possessed by a person are transferred with free consent for a price called consideration, and the conveyance must be in accordance with law so that title passes from the seller to the buyer [11]. 

For completion of the transfer:
- Tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or a reversion or other intangible thing, can be made only by a registered instrument [1].
- In the State of Assam, such transfer must be by an instrument registered in the State of Assam, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Indian Registration Act, 1908 [1].
- Tangible immovable property of a value less than one hundred rupees may be transferred either by a registered instrument or by delivery of the property [1].

rows.question: What is the difference between a condition and a warranty in a sale of goods?
queries: What is the difference between a condition and a warranty in a sale of goods?
difference between condition and warranty sale of goods stipulation treatment as warranty
Sale of Goods Act section 12 condition warranty definition
Sale of Goods Act section 13 breach of condition treated as breach of warranty
topSources: The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 s12
The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 s13
The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 s16
The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 s59
rows.answer:
A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated under Section 12 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 [1][11]. 

A warranty is a stipulation collateral to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a claim for damages but not to a right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated under Section 12 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 [1][11]. 

Whether a stipulation in a contract of sale is a condition or a warranty depends in each case on the construction of the contract, and a stipulation may be a condition even though it is called a warranty in the contract under Section 12 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 [1][11].

rows.answer:
A director of a company shall act in accordance with the articles of the company, as stated in Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 [1]. 

A director shall act in good faith to promote the objects of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, and in the best interests of the company, its employees, the shareholders, the community, and for the protection of the environment, according to Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 [1].

A director shall exercise duties with due and reasonable care, skill and diligence and shall exercise independent judgment, under Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 [1].

A director shall not involve in a situation in which the director has a direct or indirect interest that conflicts, or possibly may conflict, with the interest of the company, pursuant to Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 [1].

A director shall not achieve or attempt to achieve any undue gain or advantage either to himself or to his relatives, partners, or associates, as provided in Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 [1].

A director shall not assign office, and any assignment so made shall be void, under Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 [1].

rows.answer:
Whoever drives or attempts to drive a motor vehicle with alcohol exceeding 30 mg. per 100 ml. of blood detected by a breath analyser test, or while under the influence of a drug to such an extent as to be incapable of exercising proper control over the vehicle, is punishable for the first offence with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand rupees, or with both, and for a second or subsequent offence committed within three years of the previous similar offence with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine which may extend to three thousand rupees, or with both, under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 [1][9].

Gratuity is payable to an employee on the termination of employment after rendering continuous service for not less than five years on superannuation, retirement or resignation, or death or disablement due to accident or disease, as provided in Section 4 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 [1] and Section 53 of the Code on Social Security, 2020 [3]. The completion of continuous service of five years is not necessary where the termination is due to death or disablement under Section 4 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 [1].
